read.sections.0.heading.source: A map shows a place from above
read.sections.0.heading.back: A map shows a place from above

read.sections.0.text.note: Babylon written 'Ba-bi-lon', Marshall Islands kept as 'quần đảo Marshall' (textbooks sometimes write Mác-san), I-rắc for Iraq. 'Hải đồ' for the Marshall Islands stick chart (a sailors' chart): check it is understood by 12-year-olds; the simpler text says 'bản đồ'. The clay tablet map is described as 'tấm đất sét'.
read.sections.0.text.source: A map is a drawing of a place, usually as a bird would see it from the sky. A map cannot show everything, so the mapmaker chooses what to include. For example, a bus map shows bus stops, and a rain map shows where it rains most. People have made maps for thousands of years. About 2,500 years ago, someone in today's Iraq made a map of the world on a clay tablet. It shows the city of Babylon in the middle. In the Marshall Islands in the Pacific Ocean, sailors made charts from sticks and shells. The sticks showed how ocean waves moved, and the shells showed islands.
read.sections.0.text.back: A map is a drawing of a place, usually as if a bird were looking down from the sky. A map cannot show everything, so the mapmaker chooses what to put in. For example, a bus map shows bus stops, while a rain map shows where it rains most. People have drawn maps for thousands of years. About 2,500 years ago, someone in present-day Iraq drew a map of the world on a clay tablet. The map shows the city of Babylon right in the middle. In the Marshall Islands in the Pacific Ocean, sailors made sea charts from sticks and shells. The sticks show how the ocean waves move, and the shells show the islands.

read.sections.0.simpler.note: Check it keeps the idea that the map's maker chooses what to show.
read.sections.0.simpler.source: A map is a picture of a place. It shows the place from above, like a bird sees it. A map cannot show everything. The person who makes it picks what to show. A bus map shows bus stops. People made maps long ago too. Someone in what is now Iraq made a map on clay. Sailors in the Marshall Islands made maps with sticks and shells. The shells showed islands.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: A map is a drawing of a place. A map shows the place from above, like a bird looking down. A map cannot show everything. The mapmaker chooses what to show. A bus map shows bus stops. People in the old days drew maps too. Someone in the place that is Iraq today drew a map on clay. Sailors in the Marshall Islands made maps with sticks and shells. The shells show the islands.

read.sections.1.heading.source: Four tools help you read a map
read.sections.1.heading.back: Four tools help you read a map

read.sections.1.text.note: KEY_TERMS used: 'chú giải bản đồ' (key), 'kí hiệu' (symbol), 'tỉ lệ' (scale), 'đường đi' (route). The English says the key is also called a legend; I wrote 'hay còn gọi là bảng chú giải'. A native speaker should check that this second name is natural, and whether 'bảng chú giải' is really a different word for learners. | Review: 'hoa gió' for compass rose and 'bảng chú giải' as the second name of 'chú giải bản đồ' need a native-reader check. Both are in use in Vietnamese school geography but 'hoa gió' can also mean a wind-frequency diagram.
read.sections.1.text.source: Most maps include four tools that help you read them. The title tells you what the map is about. The key, which is also called a legend, explains each symbol. A symbol is a colour, line or shape that represents something real. On the Riverstone map, a blue line is the river, and a green square is the community centre. The compass rose shows directions, and sometimes it is simply an arrow pointing north. The scale shows how distance on the map compares with real distance. On this map, one square is 100 metres, so the four-square footpath is about 400 metres long.
read.sections.1.text.back: Most maps have four tools that help you read them. The title tells what the map is about. The map key, also called the legend (bảng chú giải), explains each symbol. A symbol is a colour, a line or a shape that stands for something real. On the Riverstone map, the blue line is the river, and the green square is the community centre. The compass rose shows directions, and sometimes it is only an arrow pointing north. The scale tells how much distance on the map equals real distance. On this map one square is 100 metres, so a walking path four squares long is about 400 metres long.

read.sections.1.simpler.note: Calculation (4 squares x 100 metres = 400 metres) is kept. Check 'Vậy nó dài khoảng 400 mét' is clear.
read.sections.1.simpler.source: Most maps have four tools. The title says what the map is about. The key tells what each symbol means. A symbol is a small shape, line or colour. It stands for a real thing. On the Riverstone map, a blue line is the river. The compass rose shows north, south, east and west. The scale helps you see how far things are. Here, one square is 100 metres. The path to the centre is four squares. So it is about 400 metres long.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: Most maps have four tools. The title tells what the map is about. The map key tells what each symbol means. A symbol is a small shape, a line or a colour. It stands for something real. On the Riverstone map, the blue line is the river. The compass rose shows north, south, east and west. The scale helps you know how far apart places are. Here, one square is 100 metres. The path to the centre is four squares long. So it is about 400 metres long.

read.sections.2.text.note: 'Người đọc bản đồ cẩn thận', 'dùng bản đồ làm bằng chứng', and 'cực kỳ hữu ích'. Check the last sentence 'nó không phải là chính nơi đó' (a map is not the place itself) is natural Vietnamese.
read.sections.2.text.source: The footpath from East Homes is about 400 metres, but the main-road route is about 700 metres, so the footpath is the shorter route. But is it the best route for every visitor? The map does not tell you if the path is muddy, if it has steps, or if it has lights at night. It also does not show whether the footbridge is open today. People who use the path every day know this information. A careful map reader uses the map as evidence and then asks local people who know the place. A map is extremely useful, but it is not the place itself.
read.sections.2.text.back: The walking path from East Homes is about 400 metres long, and the route along the main road is about 700 metres long, so the walking path is the shorter route. But is it the best route for every visitor? The map does not tell you whether the path is muddy, whether it has steps, or whether it has lights at night. The map also does not say whether the footbridge is open today. People who use this path every day know these things. A careful map reader uses the map as evidence, then asks local people who know the place well. A map is extremely useful, but it is not the place itself.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: The path over the bridge is 400 metres. The way by the road is 700 metres. So the path is the shorter route. But is it the best route? The map does not tell us everything. Is the path muddy? Does it have steps? Is it dark at night? People who walk there every day know. So look at the map first. Then ask people who know the place.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: The path over the bridge is 400 metres long. The route along the main road is 700 metres long. So the walking path is the shorter route. But is it the best route? The map does not tell us everything. Is the path muddy? Does it have steps? Is it dark at night? People who walk there every day know. So, look at the map first. Then ask people who know the place well.

watch.summary.note: Ordnance Survey is a name, kept. 'Vương quốc Anh' for 'Great Britain': strictly Great Britain is the island, not the whole United Kingdom, so a reviewer should check. Steve Backshall called 'nhà thám hiểm'. | Review: English says Ordnance Survey makes maps of 'Great Britain'; Vietnamese says 'Vương quốc Anh' (United Kingdom, which includes Northern Ireland, which OS does not map). Native reader to decide on 'nước Anh' or 'đảo Anh'.
watch.summary.source: In this short video, the explorer Steve Backshall talks about map symbols. Ordnance Survey makes maps of Great Britain. Every Ordnance Survey map has a key, which is also called a legend. The key lists the symbols and says what each one means. A symbol is a small picture, line or colour. It stands for a real thing, like a path, a river or a building. Symbols save space, so a map can show a lot in a small area. When you know the symbols, you can understand a place before you go there. Maps from other mapmakers may use different symbols. So always read the key first.
watch.summary.back: In this short video, the explorer Steve Backshall talks about map symbols. Ordnance Survey makes maps for the United Kingdom. Every Ordnance Survey map has a map key, also called a legend (bảng chú giải). The key lists the symbols and tells what each symbol means. A symbol is a small picture, a line or a colour. It stands for something real, like a path, a river or a building. Symbols save space, so a map can show many things in a small area. When you know the symbols, you can understand a place before you get there. Maps by other mapmakers may use different symbols. So always read the map key first.
